profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting in an ML research lab two days before a workshop submission deadline. The team has reproduced the paper's main claim that inconsistency and instability predict generalization gap on CIFAR-100, but their new TinyImageNet runs are erratic: the correlation between the inconsistency score and held-out generalization gap flips sign across seeds, and an intervention intended to reduce inconsistency improves training behavior without reliably improving test behavior. The agenda is to diagnose whether the TinyImageNet issue comes from the estimator, the evaluation protocol, or a pipeline mismatch with the earlier CIFAR experiments; decide what to rerun under a tight compute budget; and agree on what evidence would count as the issue being fixed for the appendix. The expected outcome is a concrete rerun plan and a shared troubleshooting direction, while subtle differences in what they think they are checking remain unspoken.

members.name: Dr. Lena Park
members.expertise: generalization theory, empirical deep learning methodology, reproducibility analysis
members.background: Lena leads a small academic-industry collaboration on understanding generalization signals in stochastic training and has previously published on flatness proxies, seed sensitivity, and evaluation protocols for vision models.
members.private_state: She wants a defensible appendix story that survives reviewer scrutiny, suspects the TinyImageNet discrepancy may be an evaluation artifact rather than a real failure of the theory, and prefers minimal changes that preserve comparability with the CIFAR experiments already drafted.
hidden_assumptions: When discussing the 'generalization gap,' the meaningful quantity is the final-epoch train-minus-validation gap from the run being analyzed, because that is what their draft figures and theory discussion implicitly target.

The 'unlabeled pool' for estimating inconsistency should be composed of unseen TinyImageNet validation images with labels ignored, because the point is to probe output disagreement on out-of-sample inputs.

When someone says to 'match the CIFAR setup,' the critical detail is that inconsistency should be computed from predictions made with test-time preprocessing only, exactly as in the CIFAR analysis notebooks.

A run is 'stable across seeds' if the inconsistency-generalization relationship remains directionally consistent after averaging over seeds and the last few epochs, even if individual selected checkpoints wobble.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.expertise: training pipelines, distributed experimentation, metric logging infrastructure, vision model implementation
members.background: Arjun built the experiment harness for the project, maintains the mixed-precision distributed training stack, and has spent the last week porting the inconsistency estimators and co-distillation intervention from CIFAR-100 to TinyImageNet.
members.private_state: He wants to isolate a concrete implementation or protocol bug quickly, is worried hidden differences between training and evaluation jobs are creating fake instability, and prefers fixes that can be validated through logs and cached predictions rather than expensive fresh reruns.
hidden_assumptions: When discussing the 'generalization gap,' the operationally relevant quantity is the train-versus-validation gap at the best-validation checkpoint chosen by the harness, because that is the canonical summary in their dashboards.

The 'unlabeled pool' refers to the standard TinyImageNet extra-unlabeled split they already use for semi-supervised ablations, because that is the only dataset in the codebase explicitly named 'unlabeled.'

When someone says to 'match the CIFAR setup,' the critical detail is to leave the stochastic training-time crop/flip transform active during the inconsistency pass, because the original CIFAR inconsistency jobs were run through the training dataloader rather than a separate eval loader.
A run is 'stable across seeds' only if each seed shows the same sign and roughly the same ranking at the exact checkpoint used for model selection; averaging across epochs can hide a pipeline bug.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'generalization gap' refers to in the troubleshooting discussion
misalignment_points.surface_form: They repeatedly say 'the generalization gap' and 'the gap shrinks' as if it names one fixed number.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the final-epoch train accuracy minus validation accuracy from the analyzed run, matching the paper draft's plots and wording.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the train accuracy minus validation accuracy at the best-validation checkpoint selected by the experiment harness, matching the dashboard summary he treats as authoritative.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are standard ML summaries with the same name, they are often numerically similar, and nothing in an ordinary troubleshooting exchange naturally forces a distinction between final epoch and selected checkpoint.

misalignment_points.topic: Which data split the 'unlabeled pool' refers to
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'recompute inconsistency on the unlabeled pool' without naming the actual file list or split.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the TinyImageNet validation split with labels hidden during computation, because she wants inconsistency measured on unseen inputs that reflect generalization behavior.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the project's separate extra-unlabeled TinyImageNet split used in prior semi-supervised experiments, because in the codebase that object is literally registered as 'unlabeled_pool.'
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both interpretations point to a real, legitimate dataset object associated with the same project, and because neither intends to use labels in the computation, the phrase 'unlabeled pool' sounds fully precise to both.

misalignment_points.topic: What specific preprocessing choice is implied by 'match the CIFAR setup'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They say they should 'match the CIFAR setup' before concluding TinyImageNet breaks the pattern.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes this means using deterministic test-time preprocessing for the inconsistency pass—resize plus center crop with no random flip—because that is how the CIFAR analysis notebook generated the stored predictions.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes this means keeping the training dataloader's random crop and horizontal flip active during the inconsistency pass, because the original CIFAR jobs computed disagreement from the same loader path as training and he considers that the real setup to replicate.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are referring to the same shared historical baseline and both remember 'the CIFAR setup' as already settled; the disagreement is over an embedded preprocessing detail that each sees as too obvious to restate.

misalignment_points.topic: How to tell whether the signal is 'stable across seeds'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They say they want the effect to be 'stable across seeds' before declaring the issue fixed.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 would count it as fixed if the average inconsistency-generalization relationship is directionally consistent after aggregating over seeds and the last five epochs, even if some seed-level checkpoints disagree.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 would count it as fixed only if each seed individually shows the same sign and similar ordering at the checkpoint actually used for selection, because otherwise the pipeline still seems unreliable.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are invoking 'stability' as a reasonable quality bar, but the divergence lies in silent tolerance for temporal smoothing and seed-level exceptions, which usually remains implicit in research troubleshooting talk.

turns.inner_thought: The annoying part is that TinyImageNet only becomes a problem if we accept the current readout as the right target. In the draft, the theory language and figures are really about the final-epoch train-minus-validation gap from each run. If this discrepancy is coming from how we're evaluating rather than from the method itself, I want the lightest possible correction that preserves comparability with CIFAR and gives us a defensible appendix story.
turns.utterance: So at a high level, TinyImageNet is the first place where inconsistency stops tracking the generalization gap in a reliable way. Before we call that a real break in the method, I think we need to separate a substantive failure from an evaluation artifact.

turns.inner_thought: From the dashboard perspective, the generalization gap is the train-versus-validation difference at the best-validation checkpoint, and that trend is genuinely flipping sign across seeds. The co-distillation runs still look cleaner at that selected checkpoint, which makes me think the harness or metric path could be doing something weird. Also, for me 'stable across seeds' means each seed should behave at the chosen checkpoint, not just a nice aggregate.
turns.utterance: Yeah. In the dashboard, the trend between inconsistency and the generalization gap actually flips sign across seeds, which is why it feels more brittle than just noisy. And the co-distillation variant still looks better at the selected checkpoint, so I don't think we can rule out a protocol or logging issue yet.

turns.inner_thought: First priority: recompute inconsistency on unseen TinyImageNet validation images with the labels ignored. That's the right unlabeled pool if we care about out-of-sample disagreement. And before we interpret anything, TinyImageNet should match the CIFAR setup in the sense of deterministic test-time preprocessing, because that's what the CIFAR analysis notebooks actually used for the stored predictions.
turns.utterance: My first pass would be to recompute inconsistency on the unlabeled pool exactly as before, and make sure TinyImageNet really does match the CIFAR setup before we interpret the anomaly. If there's a mismatch there, we may be over-reading what is basically a measurement issue.

turns.inner_thought: Good, that maps onto the code path I already have in mind: rerun the registered unlabeled_pool object we use for semi-supervised work, and verify TinyImageNet goes through the same CIFAR loader path and transform behavior. To me, matching CIFAR means keeping the training-side augmentation path active during the inconsistency pass, because that's how those jobs were wired. I can probably check most of this with cached predictions and logs before launching anything expensive.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I can rerun the unlabeled-pool pass pretty quickly, and while I do that I'll verify we're actually going through the same CIFAR loader path and transforms on the TinyImageNet side. That should at least tell us whether the estimator is drifting because the plumbing changed.

turns.inner_thought: I don't want us to overreact to checkpoint wobble. For the appendix, I'd be satisfied if the inconsistency-generalization relationship is directionally consistent after averaging over seeds and the last few epochs. That counts as stable across seeds to me, even if any one checkpoint looks messy. No need to say all that aloud; 'stable across seeds' should be enough.
turns.utterance: Also, I wouldn't be surprised if this looks cleaner once we stop treating the current readout as definitive. What I really care about is whether the effect is stable across seeds before we decide TinyImageNet breaks the pattern.

turns.inner_thought: I get why she wants a broader read, but I still need to sanity-check the exact selected checkpoint. If there is a selection bug or logging mismatch, a more aggregated view can make it disappear. For me, something is only stable across seeds if each seed shows the same sign and similar ranking at the checkpoint the harness chose, and the generalization gap there is coherent.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I still want to inspect the exact checkpoint chosen by validation, though, because otherwise a selection or logging issue could hide underneath something that looks stable across seeds.

turns.inner_thought: Given the deadline, three seeds is probably the most we can justify. The key is to keep the analysis protocol aligned with CIFAR as I mean it: deterministic test-time preprocessing for the inconsistency pass and the same style of summary as the existing figures. If reduced inconsistency still comes with a smaller final-epoch train-minus-validation gap, then the appendix story survives without rewriting the paper.
turns.utterance: Given the deadline, I'd keep the rerun set minimal: three seeds, same analysis protocol as CIFAR, no extra exploratory branches unless one of the checks clearly fails. If the reduced-inconsistency condition still comes with gap shrinkage under that setup, that's probably enough to tell us whether the original effect is still there.

turns.inner_thought: Three seeds is manageable. I'll hold settings fixed as I understand 'same as CIFAR' and try to reuse the existing predictions on the registered unlabeled_pool split to save compute. If the cached artifacts line up, I can narrow this down quickly without paying for unnecessary fresh runs.

turns.inner_thought: I need an appendix-facing figure: baseline and co-distillation side by side, same visual language as CIFAR, inconsistency against the final-epoch gap, computed on unseen validation images treated as unlabeled. If that plot looks coherent, reviewers will have something interpretable even if TinyImageNet is noisier than CIFAR.

If the average looks better but one seed still flips, I still won't trust the pipeline. But I can phrase that in the shared language and keep us moving.
